section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Haploidentical Stem Cell Transplant (Beijing Protocol)
section.intro: Haploidentical ("haplo") transplant using the Beijing Protocol offers a curative option for blood disorders when no fully matched sibling or unrelated donor is available. These FAQs explain how it works, who it may suit, and what international patients should know.

groups.title: Understanding Haploidentical Transplant and the Beijing Protocol

items.q: What is a haploidentical stem cell transplant?
items.a: A haploidentical stem cell transplant is a transplant that uses a half-matched family donor, such as a parent, child, or sibling who shares roughly 50% of tissue-typing (HLA) markers. It allows patients without a fully matched sibling or unrelated donor to still receive curative transplant. Because nearly every patient has a half-matched relative, this approach greatly widens donor access. Suitability depends on diagnosis, disease status, organ health, and specialist review.

The Beijing Protocol is a specific method of performing haploidentical transplant developed at Peking University in China. It uses granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) to prime the donor, combined with intensive immune-suppressing medicines, instead of removing certain immune cells from the graft. This "GIAC" approach aims to reduce graft-versus-host disease while preserving engraftment. Reported outcomes in selected patients are encouraging, though results depend on disease type, age, and overall health.

items.q: How does the Beijing Protocol differ from post-transplant cyclophosphamide?
items.a: The Beijing Protocol and post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) are two different strategies for the same goal of safe half-matched transplant. The Beijing Protocol uses G-CSF-primed grafts with strong upfront immunosuppression, while PTCy gives high-dose cyclophosphamide shortly after transplant to remove reactive immune cells. Both aim to lower graft-versus-host disease. The choice depends on the transplant centre's experience, the patient's condition, and specialist judgment rather than one method being universally superior.

items.q: Which conditions can be treated with haploidentical transplant?
items.a: Haploidentical transplant may be considered for several blood cancers and inherited blood disorders, including acute leukaemia, thalassaemia, aplastic anaemia, sickle cell disease, and certain immune deficiencies. It is often explored when a disease is curable by transplant but no matched sibling or unrelated donor is available. Whether it is appropriate depends on diagnosis, disease stage, prior treatment, organ function, and evaluation by an experienced transplant team.

items.q: Who is eligible for a haploidentical transplant?
items.a: Haploidentical transplant may be suitable for selected patients who need a curative transplant but lack a fully matched donor. Eligibility depends on the underlying disease, disease control, age, organ function, infection status, and overall fitness. A suitable half-matched relative willing to donate is also required. Final eligibility is decided only after detailed testing and assessment by a transplant specialist, and not every patient will be a candidate.

items.q: Who can be a half-matched donor?
items.a: A half-matched donor is usually a close blood relative who shares one HLA haplotype, most often a parent, child, or a sibling who is not a full match. Because children inherit half their tissue type from each parent, most patients have at least one available haploidentical donor. Donors are chosen after HLA typing and health screening, considering factors such as age, sex, blood group, and donor-specific antibodies identified during testing.

items.q: How does the transplant process work?
items.a: The haploidentical transplant process begins with conditioning chemotherapy, sometimes with radiation, to prepare the body and suppress the immune system. The donor then receives G-CSF to mobilise stem cells, which are collected and infused into the patient. Under the Beijing Protocol, immune-suppressing medicines follow to reduce graft-versus-host disease. Engraftment usually takes two to four weeks, with close monitoring for infection and complications throughout a hospital stay that often lasts several weeks.

items.q: What are the main risks and side effects?
items.a: The main risks of haploidentical transplant include graft-versus-host disease, where donor cells attack the patient's tissues, along with infections, low blood counts, organ toxicity, and graft failure. Because the donor is only half-matched, careful immune management is essential. Risks vary with age, disease, and health status. These complications should be discussed thoroughly with the transplant team, who take steps to prevent, monitor, and treat them during recovery.

Outcomes of haploidentical transplant have improved substantially, and in selected patients results can approach those of matched-donor transplants. Success depends heavily on the underlying disease, disease control before transplant, patient age, organ function, and centre experience. Some patients achieve long-term cure, while others face relapse or complications. No transplant guarantees a specific outcome, so realistic expectations should be discussed with the treating team based on each individual's situation.

items.q: How long is recovery after a haploidentical transplant?
items.a: Recovery after haploidentical transplant is gradual and varies between patients. The early hospital phase usually lasts three to six weeks until blood counts recover. Immune recovery, however, can take six months to over a year, during which infection precautions, medications, and frequent follow-up are needed. Some patients return to normal activities within several months, while others need longer. The pace depends on complications, graft-versus-host disease, and overall health, guided by the medical team.

items.q: How much does a haploidentical transplant cost?
items.a: The cost of a haploidentical transplant varies widely by country, hospital, and patient condition, and firm figures cannot be promised in advance. In India it is often more affordable than in Western countries, while China and other centres have their own pricing. Final cost depends on diagnosis, conditioning regimen, length of stay, complications, medicines, and follow-up care. A personalised estimate should be obtained after the hospital reviews the patient's medical records.

items.q: Is haploidentical transplant available in India?
items.a: Yes, haploidentical transplant is available at several experienced transplant centres in India, and both Beijing Protocol and post-transplant cyclophosphamide approaches are used. India is a common destination for international patients seeking transplant due to specialised units and relatively lower costs. Availability for a specific patient depends on hospital acceptance, donor suitability, disease status, and medical review. Admission and timing are confirmed only after the transplant team evaluates the case.

items.q: Which countries offer the Beijing Protocol?
items.a: The Beijing Protocol originated in China, where it is widely performed, and versions of haploidentical transplant using this or similar approaches are now offered in India and several other countries. Centre experience varies, so outcomes can differ between hospitals. Choosing where to have treatment depends on donor availability, cost, travel feasibility, and the expertise of the transplant unit. A specialist can advise which options may be appropriate for a particular patient.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for haploidentical transplant?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials continue to study haploidentical transplant, including refinements of the Beijing Protocol, graft-versus-host disease prevention, and combinations with cellular or gene therapies. Trials may offer access to newer strategies but have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Enrolment is never guaranteed and is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment. Patients interested in trials should discuss eligibility, potential risks, and expected commitments with their oncology team.

items.q: How does haploidentical transplant compare with gene therapy for inherited blood disorders?
items.a: Haploidentical transplant and gene therapy are both potentially curative for inherited blood disorders such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease, but they work differently. Transplant replaces the patient's blood system with a donor's cells, while gene therapy modifies the patient's own cells so no donor is needed. Each carries distinct risks, costs, and availability. The most suitable option depends on the specific condition, age, donor access, and specialist evaluation.

items.q: Can haploidentical transplant be used when other donors are unavailable?
items.a: Haploidentical transplant is often chosen specifically when a fully matched sibling or unrelated donor cannot be found, which is common for patients from ethnic backgrounds underrepresented in donor registries. Because a half-matched relative is available for nearly everyone, it removes long waits for registry searches and allows transplant to proceed sooner when time matters. Whether it is the best route still depends on disease urgency, donor health, and specialist assessment.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to plan a haploidentical transplant abroad?
items.a: To plan a haploidentical transplant abroad, transplant teams typically need recent diagnosis details, bone marrow or biopsy reports, blood counts, HLA typing of the patient and potential donors, imaging, and a summary of previous treatments. Information on organ function and infection screening is also important. Complete, up-to-date records allow accurate assessment and a realistic cost estimate. The treating centre confirms what is required before offering an opinion or admission.

items.q: How can international patients access haploidentical transplant?
items.a: International patients can access haploidentical transplant by sending medical records to an experienced centre for review, arranging donor testing, and obtaining an estimate and treatment plan. Access depends on hospital acceptance, donor suitability, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's condition, none of which can be guaranteed in advance. Planning should also cover the extended stay for recovery and arrangements for follow-up care after returning home.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with haploidentical stem cell transplant?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant transplant specialists or centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, donor evaluation, appointments, travel, visa support, and follow-up care. It supports patients seeking haploidentical transplant across different countries and centres. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology and transplant team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, disease status, donor options, previous treatment, and overall health, and outcomes are never guaranteed.
